name: Sango
confidence_why: Samarin's grammar (1963, published 1967), the only first-hand description of Sango stress, says stress is not phonemic and only sometimes occurs for expressive effect, falling on the first syllable when it does, and his 1967 Basic Course tells learners not to stress any syllable, so the fixed: initial syllable label taken over from Gordon 2002 and StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz & van der Hulst 2015) captures the placement but overstates the type, while Jacquot 1960 treats Bangui Sango purely as a three-tone language and says nothing about stress.

It seems to be in no way correlated with intonation contours but occurs on any word regardless of its class. This being true, it is difficult to determine why stress sometimes occurs at all. ... tone_statements.citation: Bordal, Guri. 2012. Prosodie et contact de langues: le cas du système tonal du français centrafricain. Thèse de doctorat (PhD), Universitetet i Oslo & Université Paris Ouest Nanterre La Défense (MoDyCo). 206 pp. HAL tel-00789349.
tone_statements.quote: La variété de sango la plus répandue à Bangui possède trois tons de registre et deux tons modulés (Diki-Kidiri, c.p.). [...] Tout comme en ngbandi (cf. chapitre 1, §1.2), les tons lexicaux en sango ont une fonction distinctive. Cependant, il y a une différence entre le sango et sa langue mère : le ngbandi marque à la fois certaines catégories grammaticales d’un point de vue tonal et distingue des paires minimales, tandis qu’en sango moderne, le marquage tonal des phénomènes grammaticaux a disparu. [...] La sango n’a pas d’accent lexical, ni d’accent tonal, les deux traits dont la description exige le recours au système métrique.
tone_statements.translation: The most widespread variety of Sango in Bangui has three register tones and two contour tones (Diki-Kidiri, p.c.). [...] Just as in Ngbandi, the lexical tones of Sango have a distinctive function. However, there is a difference between Sango and its mother language: Ngbandi both marks certain grammatical categories tonally and distinguishes minimal pairs, whereas in modern Sango the tonal marking of grammatical phenomena has disappeared. [...] Sango has no lexical accent, nor tonal accent, the two features whose description requires recourse to the metrical system.
tone_statements.locator: ch. 3 §2.1 'Système de tons lexicaux' with Tableau 7 (p. 57), §2.1.1 'Fonction' (p. 58), and the metrical remark at the end of §2 (p. 65)
tone_statements.n_tones: 3 level (L, M, H) + 2 contour (HL, LH; ~2% of words, treated as sequences)

tone_statements.quote: [p.861] Sango is derived from a language which consists of closely related dialects called Ngbandi, Yakoma, Dendi, and Sango (see the map) ... [p.865] Sango has three phonemic tones: high, mid, and low. ... [pp.875-876] In comparison with the phonological features common to Adamawa-Ubangian languages (Boyd 1989), Pidgin Sango is a typical central African language: it has a 7-vowel system, 3 tones, and a basically CV syllable structure. It is atypical in its lack of morphophonemic use of tone and its lack of contour tones. The lack of morphemic tone is understandable in a situation of pidginization: the morphotonemics of the various substrate languages are not identical

readall_conflicts: No direct conflict between opened sources, because only one was opened. The catalog's initial-stress rule (src StressTyp2) is neither supported nor contradicted by Jacquot 1960, which treats Bangui Sango purely as a three-register tone language and never uses the word 'accent'. As context only (not a listed work, but already held by the project in the same folder): Samarin's 1967 ERIC Basic Course in Sango (lesson on tone) tells learners to 'Avoid stressing one syllable more than the others' and warns that an English speaker 'will be inclined to stress the first or second syllables of polysyllabic Sango words' because he hears high tone as main stress, which sits uneasily with a fixed: initial syllable stress record for Sango; that source should be opened properly before the catalog record is changed.

audit.recode_to: no lexical/obligatory word stress (tone language; sporadic expressive stress, which when present falls on the first syllable) -- or, if the scheme has no such class, keep 'initial' but drop strict/dominant and add a caution flag 'expressive, non-obligatory (Samarin 1963:1, 28)'
audit.reasoning: Sourcing itself is solid: the deciding text is Samarin's reference grammar (1963 typescript = 1967 Mouton), held in full with a text, and both quoted passages are verbatim at p.1 and §3.30 p.28 (p.54). The risk is in the reading, not the source. Samarin files stress under Intonation, says twice that it is 'not a significant feature of the phonemic structure', 'not lexically significant', 'used expressively', and that 'it is difficult to determine why stress sometimes occurs at all'; the initial-syllable statement describes where this optional expressive prominence lands when it occurs. His 1967 Basic Course (downloaded now, ERIC ED018784) instructs learners to avoid stressing any syllable and explains that English speakers mis-hear high tone as stress; his 2013 APiCS sketch (downloaded now) describes three tone levels and never mentions stress. sources.quote: 'Sango has three levels of pitch, as does Ngbandi ... Pitch features in only a few words to differentiate lexemes and has very little role in grammar ... Questions are not ordinarily marked by a special feature of pitch, but when a question is repeated or when expressing emotion, a rising-falling contour with greater emphasis occurs on the final syllable.' No mention of word stress anywhere in the chapter.

sources.note: No tone inventory and no statement of the tone system: 'Elements de phonologie' (p. 1) treats only vowels (French front rounded vowels and schwa absent; nasal vowels in, en, an, on, un). Tone is presupposed by the fully tone-marked 1984 orthography used in all examples (a = L, a-dieresis = M, a-circumflex = H) and by one grammatical-tone statement in the verb section (p. 3): 'Le virtuel est marque par un ton haut (note par un accent circonflexe) sur le pronom sujet ou le prefixe verbal a-.' Nothing on stress or intonation.

sources.note: Per the English Wikipedia tone section that cites its phonology chapter: Sango has three basic tones (high, mid, low) with contour tones mostly in French loans, tones carry a low functional load though minimal pairs exist (dü 'give birth' vs dû 'hole'), isolated-word tones vary idiolectally and with speakers' L1; the official orthography leaves L unmarked, marks M with diaeresis and H with circumflex; nominalising -ngö levels verb tones to mid. To be verified in the thesis itself.
